hook.situation: You're at a Korean café. You want water, a croissant, and you want to pay by card. You manage to say '물 주세요' — but then you freeze. How do you add 'and the croissant too'? How do you ask if card payment is okay? You need three small but powerful particles: 도 (also), 만 (only), and 로/으로 (by means of).
objectives: Use 도 to add one more item to an order ('and this too, please')
Use 만 to set a limit ('only this, nothing else')
Use 로/으로 to express payment method, transport, or language ('by card', 'in Korean')
hook.whyItMatters: These three particles unlock real transactions. 도, 만, and 로/으로 are used in every café, restaurant, and convenience store interaction in Korea. Without them, every order is a single isolated item — with them, you can build natural, flexible requests that sound like a real customer, not a tourist reading a phrasebook.

grammarNotes.title: 도 vs. 만 — Adding vs. Limiting
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 도 as a SHOPPING CART and 만 as a SPOTLIGHT. 도 throws one more thing into the cart — it adds to what already exists. 만 shines a spotlight on one single item and says everything else is in the dark. Same menu, opposite choices.

examples.note: 도 follows the item being added — 이것 gets tossed into the cart alongside whatever was ordered before
만 follows 물 — the spotlight is on water alone; no food, no other drinks
도 after a pronoun — the speaker is adding themselves to the group of people ordering
만 after a time word — the discount spotlight shines on today only, not tomorrow
도 in a question — asking whether coffee joins the list of drinks the person has

a.en: This too, please. (I want this in addition to what I already ordered.)

b.en: Only this, please. (Just this. Nothing else at all.)

contrastPairs.explanation: Same object (이것), completely different meaning. 도 = add to the order. 만 = limit the order to just this. In a convenience store, 이것도 주세요 means 'and this on top'; 이것만 주세요 means 'cancel everything else, just give me this.'

a.en: I eat too. (Other people eat, and so do I.)

b.en: Only I eat. (Nobody else eats — just me.)

contrastPairs.explanation: 도 makes you part of the group. 만 isolates you as the sole person. The verb is identical; the particle creates the entire contrast.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers try to keep 는 (the topic marker) and add 도 on top of it, but 도 replaces subject and topic particles — not joins them. Say 저도, never 저는도. The same rule applies to 만: 물만 주세요, never 물을만 주세요.

exceptions: 도 and 만 can follow location particles in special cases: 학교에서도 (at school too), 서울에서만 (only in Seoul) — here 도/만 follow 에서, not replace it
만 can attach to time expressions naturally: 한 번만 (just once), 5분만 (just five minutes)

grammarNotes.title: 로 / 으로 — Method, Means, and Direction
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 로/으로 as a CHANNEL SELECTOR. You're pointing at the channel through which the action flows: pay through the card channel, travel through the subway channel, speak through the Korean channel. Whatever you attach 로/으로 to is the channel being selected.
grammarNotes.formation: Noun + 로 (after vowel or ㄹ) | Noun + 으로 (after most consonants)

examples.note: 카드 ends in a vowel (드) → 로. Payment flows through the card channel.
지하철 ends in ㄹ → 로 (the ㄹ rule). Transit flows through the subway channel.
Language use: the communication flows through the Korean-language channel. 어 ends in a vowel → 로.
펜 ends in a consonant (ㄴ) → 으로. Writing flows through the pen channel.
현금 ends in a consonant (ㅁ) → 으로. Paying flows through the cash channel.

a.en: I go to the subway. (destination: I'm heading TO the subway station.)

b.en: I go by subway. (method: I use the subway to get there.)

contrastPairs.explanation: 에 marks the destination of movement. 로/으로 marks the channel/method used. 지하철에 가요 means you're going to the subway (maybe to pick someone up); 지하철로 가요 means the subway is your transport method.

a.en: I buy it by card. (method of payment)

b.en: I buy a card. (card is the object being bought)

contrastPairs.explanation: 로/으로 = the card is the payment method. 를 = the card is what you're purchasing. Same noun, different particles, completely different shopping situation.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'pay by card' uses 'by', but learners often reach for 에 (which marks locations/times). 에 would suggest you're paying AT the card, as if the card were a place. 로/으로 is the method particle. Whenever you'd say 'by', 'with', 'using', or 'in (a language)' — that's 로/으로 territory.

exceptions: After ㄹ endings, use 로 not 으로: 서울로 가요 (not 서울으로), 지하철로 (not 지하철으로)
Direction meaning (toward): 집으로 가요 can also mean 'heading toward home' — context usually makes it clear whether it's method or direction

exampleSentence.note: N + 주세요 = the single most useful ordering pattern in Korea
이거 (this) + 얼마예요 — the go-to price question in any market, convenience store, or café
카드 ends in a vowel → 로 (not 으로)
현금 ends in a consonant (ㅁ) → 으로

exampleSentence.en: Is it okay to pay by card?
exampleSentence.note: 결제하다 is the formal word for payment processing; 내다 or 계산하다 are more casual
Direct N 주세요 request — no extra particles needed
주문하다 + 아/어도 돼요? = polite permission request; 받다 (receive) is often said by staff: 주문받겠습니다
메뉴 is a loanword from English; in practice many Korean cafés have menus only on boards, so this is more useful than it sounds
Quantities in ordering use native Korean numbers (하나, 둘, 셋), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼)
좀 softens the request; 좀 주세요 sounds more polite and natural than 주세요 alone
더 = more quantity; often combined with 좀 for a polite, natural request for a refill
카드 돼요? is a spoken shortcut — grammatically incomplete but perfectly natural in shops
이거 is the spoken form, 이것 is written/formal; both work at a café or shop counter
포장 (packing) = takeout in Korean. 포장이요? is how staff ask if you want it to go
추천 없어요? or 추천 메뉴요? are very natural ways to ask a café or restaurant what's good
할인 + 돼요? is the pattern to ask about discounts; 학생 할인, 앱 할인, 포인트 할인 all work the same way
맵게 is the adverbial form (spicily); 안 맵게 해 주세요 = make it in a not-spicy way — practical for dietary restrictions

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun and his coworker Yuna go to a café. Minjun orders for both of them.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Welcome! What can I get you?
lines.grammarNote: 뭐 드릴까요? — the polite 'what shall I offer you?' form staff use in Korean cafés; 드리다 is the honorific of 주다

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.grammarNote: N 주세요 ordering pattern; 두 잔 = two cups using native Korean number 두 + counter 잔

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.grammarNote: 더 (more/else) here asks if there's anything to add — functions like 도 in a question context

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.grammarNote: 크루아상 + 도 = adding the croissant to the cart (SHOPPING CART rule); 하나 = one (native Korean number)

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.ko: 저는 케이크만 주세요. 커피는 안 마셔요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun keikuman juseyo. Keopineun an masyeoyo.
lines.en: Just cake for me, please. I don't drink coffee.
lines.grammarNote: 케이크 + 만 = spotlight on cake alone (SPOTLIGHT rule); this is 만 as a dietary/preference restriction

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Got it. How would you like to pay?
lines.grammarNote: 어떻게 (how) + 하시겠어요? is the polite 'how will you do X?' frame — staff asking the payment method opens the 로/으로 response

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: I'll pay by card. Card is okay, right?
lines.grammarNote: 카드 + 로 = the CHANNEL SELECTOR (method particle); 카드 ends in vowel 드 → 로, not 으로

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, card is fine. Do you need a receipt?
lines.grammarNote: 카드로 돼요 — 로/으로 again confirming payment method; 영수증 주세요 is the natural follow-up if you want the receipt

readingText.title: 편의점에서 (At the Convenience Store)
readingText.body: 오늘 퇴근 후에 편의점에 들렀어요. 직원한테 '이거 얼마예요?' 라고 물었어요. 삼천 원이라고 했어요. 현금이 없어서 카드로 계산했어요. 영수증도 받았어요. 친구한테 선물로 과자를 사서 이것만 담았어요. 다음에는 카드 할인도 확인해야겠어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: After work today I stopped by a convenience store. I asked the staff 'How much is this?' They said it was 3,000 won. I didn't have cash so I paid by card. I got a receipt too. I bought snacks as a gift for my friend, so I put only those in the basket. Next time I should check for card discounts too.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How did the speaker pay, and why?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 카드로 계산했어요 — they paid by card because they had no cash (현금이 없어서)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What did the speaker buy, and for whom?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 친구한테 선물로 과자를 샀어요 — they bought snacks as a gift (선물로 = using the gift channel/purpose) for a friend

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every 도 and 만 in the text. For each one, explain whether it is adding something or limiting something.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 영수증도 받았어요 — 도 adds the receipt to the list of things that happened (CART: one more item); 이것만 담았어요 — 만 limits the basket contents to only the snacks (SPOTLIGHT: nothing else); 카드 할인도 확인해야겠어요 — 도 adds checking discounts to next time's plan (CART: another thing to do)

culturalNote.title: 카드 돼요? — Why Korean shops sometimes say no
culturalNote.body: In Korea, the question '카드 돼요?' (Is card okay?) is completely natural and expected. Unlike many countries where card payment is assumed, some Korean small businesses — street food stalls, traditional markets, very small local cafés — are cash-only. The reason is often the transaction fee the business pays to the card company. When you hear '현금만 돼요' (cash only), don't be surprised. It's also common to see signs like '카드 최소 금액 3,000원' (minimum card purchase 3,000 won). Having small bills (천 원, 오천 원) on hand is still a practical tip for exploring traditional markets like Gwangjang or Namdaemun.

inlineExercises.prompt: 아메리카노 주세요. 케이크___ 주세요. (I want an Americano. Cake too, please.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 adds the cake to the order (SHOPPING CART — one more item). If you used 만, the sentence would mean 'only cake, please' — cancelling the Americano you just ordered.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 물___ 마셔요. 다른 건 필요 없어요. (I drink only water. I don't need anything else.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 is the SPOTLIGHT — it limits the sentence to water and excludes everything else. 도 would mean 'I drink water too (among other things)', which contradicts '다른 건 필요 없어요'.

inlineExercises.prompt: 카드___ 결제할 수 있어요? (Can I pay by card?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 로/으로 marks the method (CHANNEL SELECTOR). 카드에 would mean 'on the card' or 'at the card' as if the card were a location, which makes no sense. The payment flows through the card channel → 카드로.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는도 주문할게요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 replaces subject and topic particles — it does not sit after them. 저는 + 도 is a double-particle error; drop 는 and say 저도. The same principle applies to 만: never 이것을만, always 이것만.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I'll pay in cash. Receipt too, please.'
inlineExercises.hint: 현금 ends in a consonant → which form? And are you adding the receipt (CART) or limiting to only the receipt (SPOTLIGHT)?

inlineExercises.prompt: The staff asks how you want to pay. You want to ask 'Is it okay if I pay by card?' Which is the most natural?
inlineExercises.explanation: 로/으로 marks the method of payment — the card is the CHANNEL. 카드에 would mean 'at the card' (card as a location — doesn't work). 카드를 would mean 'pay the card' — as if the card itself is the thing being paid, not the payment method.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배고파요? 이거___ 드세요. 다른 건 없어요. (Are you hungry? Have just this. There's nothing else.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 is the SPOTLIGHT — the context confirms there's nothing else ('다른 건 없어요'), so 만 is correct. 도 would imply there are other options too, which contradicts the sentence.

bullets: 도 = SHOPPING CART: adds one more item or person to what already exists. Replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를 — never stacks on top of them.
만 = SPOTLIGHT: limits the sentence to exactly one thing, excluding everything else. Place it directly after the word you want to isolate.
로/으로 = CHANNEL SELECTOR: marks the method, means, or tool of an action. Use 로 after vowels or ㄹ; use 으로 after other consonants.
